glossary.artificial intelligence: Software that performs tasks usually needing human judgement, such as recognising images, understanding language or making predictions.
glossary.generative AI: AI that produces new text, images, audio, video or code from a prompt, rather than only classifying or predicting.
glossary.artificial general intelligence: A hypothetical AI able to match people across most intellectual tasks. There is no agreed test for it, so labs use the term loosely.
glossary.superintelligence: A hypothetical AI that far exceeds human ability in most fields. Some labs now name teams and goals after it.
glossary.AI alignment: Research into making AI systems pursue the goals their designers and users intend, and behave safely when those goals are unclear.
glossary.AI safety: The work of preventing AI systems from causing accidental or deliberate harm, from biased outputs to misuse and loss of control.
glossary.red teaming: Deliberately attacking a model or system to find harmful behaviour or security holes before release.
glossary.deepfake: Synthetic audio, image or video made with AI to show a real person saying or doing something they did not.
glossary.inference: Running a trained model to get an answer. Most of the cost of serving AI to users is inference, not training.
glossary.compute: Shorthand for the processing power, usually GPUs or other accelerators, used to train and run AI models.
glossary.machine learning: A branch of AI in which systems learn patterns from data instead of following rules written by hand.
glossary.deep learning: Machine learning with neural networks that have many layers; the basis of modern image, speech and language models.
glossary.neural network: A model built from layers of simple connected units whose weights are adjusted during training to map inputs to outputs.
glossary.transformer: The neural network architecture, introduced in 2017, that uses attention to process whole sequences at once. Nearly all large language models are transformers.
glossary.attention: The mechanism that lets a transformer weigh how relevant every other token is when processing each token.
glossary.parameters: The learned numbers (weights) inside a model. Model size is usually quoted in parameters, for example 70B for 70 billion.
glossary.training: The process of adjusting a model's parameters on data so that its outputs improve on an objective.
glossary.pretraining: The first, most expensive training stage, in which a model learns general patterns from a very large dataset such as web text.
glossary.supervised learning: Training on examples that come with the correct answer, such as images labelled with what they show.
glossary.self-supervised learning: Training in which the data supplies its own labels, for example predicting the next word of a sentence. It is how language models are pretrained.
glossary.reinforcement learning: Training an agent by trial and error, rewarding actions that lead to good outcomes.
glossary.RLHF: Reinforcement learning from human feedback: tuning a model towards answers that human raters prefer.
glossary.fine-tuning: Further training a pretrained model on a smaller, specific dataset to adapt it to a task, style or domain.
glossary.LoRA: Low-rank adaptation: a cheap fine-tuning method that trains small add-on matrices instead of all of a model's weights.
glossary.quantization: Storing a model's weights with fewer bits, such as 8 or 4 instead of 16, so it runs faster and in less memory at a small cost in quality.
glossary.distillation: Training a smaller student model to imitate a larger teacher model's outputs.
glossary.mixture of experts: A model design in which only some sub-networks (experts) are used for each token, so a very large model costs less to run.
glossary.diffusion model: A generative model that learns to turn random noise into an image, video or audio clip by removing noise step by step.
glossary.embedding: A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text or an image, so similar items sit close together.
glossary.overfitting: When a model learns its training data too closely, including noise, and performs worse on new data.
glossary.gradient descent: The optimisation method used to train neural networks: repeatedly nudging weights in the direction that reduces error.
glossary.backpropagation: The algorithm that computes how much each weight contributed to an error, so gradient descent knows how to adjust it.
glossary.benchmark: A fixed test set used to compare models on a task. Scores can mislead when models have seen the test data during training.
glossary.scaling laws: Observed regularities showing that model performance improves predictably as data, parameters and compute grow.
glossary.synthetic data: Training data generated by models or simulations rather than collected from the real world.
glossary.interpretability: Research into what happens inside a model, so its decisions can be understood and checked.
glossary.computer vision: The field of AI that interprets images and video: recognising objects, faces, text and scenes.
glossary.natural language processing: The field of AI that deals with understanding and generating human language.
glossary.world model: A model that learns how an environment behaves so it can predict what happens next; used in robotics, games and video generation.
glossary.perplexity (metric): A measure of how surprised a language model is by text; lower means it predicts the text better.
glossary.large language model: A neural network trained on vast amounts of text to predict the next token, which lets it answer questions, write and code.
glossary.foundation model: A large model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks, rather than built for one.
glossary.frontier model: One of the most capable models available at a given time, usually from a handful of well-funded labs.
glossary.token: The unit of text a language model reads and writes, often a word or part of one. Prices and limits are counted in tokens.
glossary.tokenizer: The component that splits text into tokens and maps them to numbers before a model sees them.
glossary.context window: The maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, that a model can consider at once, including the conversation so far.
glossary.prompt: The instructions and input given to a language model.
glossary.system prompt: Standing instructions set by the developer that shape how a model behaves for every message in a conversation.
glossary.prompt engineering: Writing and testing prompts to get more reliable results from a language model.
glossary.prompt injection: An attack in which text hidden in a document, web page or email tricks a model into ignoring its instructions.
glossary.jailbreak: A prompt crafted to make a model bypass its safety rules.
glossary.hallucination: When a model states something false or invented with confidence, such as a fake citation.
glossary.retrieval-augmented generation: Fetching relevant documents and adding them to the prompt so a model answers from that material instead of memory alone.
glossary.vector database: A database that stores embeddings and finds the items most similar to a query; often used for retrieval-augmented generation.
glossary.post-training: Training after pretraining, such as instruction tuning and RLHF, that turns a raw model into a helpful assistant.
glossary.instruction tuning: Fine-tuning on examples of instructions and good responses so a model follows requests.
glossary.reasoning model: A language model trained to work through a problem step by step before answering, trading time and tokens for accuracy.
glossary.chain of thought: The intermediate reasoning steps a model writes out before its final answer.
glossary.test-time compute: Spending more computation while answering, for example by reasoning longer, to get better results without retraining.
glossary.temperature: A setting that controls randomness in a model's output: low values give predictable answers, high values give varied ones.
glossary.AI agent: A system in which a model plans and takes actions, such as using tools, browsing or editing files, to complete a goal over several steps.
glossary.tool use: A model's ability to call external functions or services, such as search, code execution or an API, and use the results.
glossary.Model Context Protocol: An open standard, introduced by Anthropic, for connecting AI assistants to tools and data sources through MCP servers.
glossary.evals: Tests that measure how well a model or AI product does on the tasks that matter to its users.
glossary.SWE-bench: A benchmark that asks models to fix real bugs from open-source GitHub projects; widely cited for coding ability.
glossary.MMLU: Massive Multitask Language Understanding: a multiple-choice test across 57 subjects, now close to saturated by top models.
glossary.open weights: A model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run, even if its training data and code are not.
glossary.multimodal model: A model that handles more than one kind of input or output, such as text, images, audio and video.
glossary.small language model: A compact language model designed to run cheaply or on a device such as a phone or laptop.
glossary.vibe coding: Building software by describing what you want to an AI coding tool and accepting its code with little manual review.
glossary.coding agent: An AI agent that reads a codebase, edits files, runs commands and tests to complete programming tasks.
glossary.latency: How long a model takes to respond; often split into time to first token and tokens per second.
glossary.semiconductor: A material such as silicon whose conductivity can be controlled; also the industry's word for chips made from it.
glossary.GPU: Graphics processing unit: a chip with thousands of small cores, first built for graphics and now the workhorse of AI training and inference.
glossary.CPU: Central processing unit: the general-purpose processor that runs a computer's operating system and most software.
glossary.NPU: Neural processing unit: a block of a chip specialised for AI calculations, common in phones and laptops.
glossary.TPU: Tensor processing unit: Google's custom AI accelerator, used in its data centres and rented through Google Cloud.
glossary.ASIC: Application-specific integrated circuit: a chip designed for one job, such as AI inference or bitcoin mining.
glossary.FPGA: Field-programmable gate array: a chip whose logic can be reconfigured after manufacture.
glossary.system on a chip: A single chip that combines CPU, GPU, memory controllers and other parts, as in most phones.
glossary.HBM: High-bandwidth memory: stacked DRAM placed next to an AI accelerator to feed it data very quickly; a supply bottleneck for AI chips.
glossary.DRAM: Dynamic random-access memory: the main working memory in computers and servers.
glossary.NAND flash: The non-volatile memory used in SSDs, phones and memory cards.
glossary.foundry: A company that manufactures chips designed by others, such as TSMC.
glossary.fabless: A chip company that designs chips but outsources manufacturing to a foundry, such as Nvidia, AMD or Qualcomm.
glossary.wafer: A thin disc of silicon on which many chips are made at once before being cut apart.
glossary.process node: A label for a generation of chipmaking technology, such as 3nm or 2nm. Smaller numbers mean denser chips, though no longer a literal size.
glossary.EUV lithography: Extreme ultraviolet lithography: the technique, using machines made only by ASML, that prints the finest features on leading-edge chips.
glossary.High-NA EUV: The newest generation of EUV machines, with a larger numerical aperture that prints even smaller features.
glossary.chiplet: A small die combined with others in one package to build a larger chip, instead of making one huge die.
glossary.advanced packaging: Techniques such as TSMC's CoWoS that place chips and memory close together in one package; a key constraint on AI chip supply.
glossary.transistor: The tiny electronic switch that chips are built from; modern chips hold billions.
glossary.gate-all-around: A transistor design in which the gate surrounds the channel on all sides, used at 2nm-class nodes.
glossary.RISC-V: An open, royalty-free instruction set architecture that anyone can use to design processors.
glossary.Arm architecture: The instruction set licensed by Arm Holdings that powers almost all phones and a growing share of laptops and servers.
glossary.x86: The instruction set used by Intel and AMD processors in most PCs and servers.
glossary.chip yield: The share of chips on a wafer that work. Low yields make new process nodes expensive.
glossary.tape-out: The point at which a chip design is finished and sent for manufacturing.
glossary.EDA: Electronic design automation: the software, from firms such as Synopsys and Cadence, used to design chips.
glossary.Moore's law: Gordon Moore's observation that the number of transistors on a chip doubles about every two years.
glossary.export controls: Government rules that restrict selling certain technology, such as advanced chips or chipmaking tools, to some countries.
glossary.data centre: A building full of servers, storage and networking. AI data centres need large amounts of power and cooling.
glossary.hyperscaler: One of the largest cloud providers, such as Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud.
glossary.NVLink: Nvidia's high-speed link for connecting GPUs to each other inside a server or rack.
glossary.silicon carbide: A semiconductor material used for power chips in electric vehicles and chargers because it handles high voltages efficiently.
glossary.bull market: A prolonged rise in prices; often defined as a 20% gain from a recent low.
glossary.bear market: A prolonged fall in prices; often defined as a 20% drop from a recent high.
glossary.correction: A fall of 10% or more from a recent peak that is smaller than a bear market.
glossary.market capitalisation: A company's share price multiplied by its number of shares: what the market values the whole company at.
glossary.price-to-earnings ratio: Share price divided by earnings per share; a common gauge of how expensive a stock is.
glossary.earnings per share: A company's profit divided by its number of shares.
glossary.dividend: A cash payment a company makes to shareholders out of its profits.
glossary.share buyback: When a company buys its own shares, reducing the number outstanding.
glossary.index: A basket of stocks tracked as one number, such as the S&P 500 or Nifty 50, used to measure the market.
glossary.ETF: Exchange-traded fund: a fund that trades on an exchange like a share, usually tracking an index or commodity.
glossary.bond yield: The return an investor earns on a bond at its current price. Yields rise when bond prices fall.
glossary.Treasury yield: The yield on US government debt. The 10-year yield is a benchmark for mortgages and borrowing worldwide.
glossary.yield curve: A chart of bond yields across maturities. When short-term yields exceed long-term ones it is called inverted, often read as a recession warning.
glossary.basis point: One hundredth of a percentage point: 25 basis points is 0.25%.
glossary.federal funds rate: The overnight interest rate the US Federal Reserve targets; its main policy tool.
glossary.FOMC: Federal Open Market Committee: the Federal Reserve body that sets US interest rates, meeting eight times a year.
glossary.quantitative easing: A central bank buying bonds to push down long-term interest rates and add money to the financial system.
glossary.quantitative tightening: A central bank shrinking its bond holdings, the reverse of quantitative easing.
glossary.inflation: The rate at which prices rise across the economy, reducing what money can buy.
glossary.CPI: Consumer price index: a measure of the prices households pay for a basket of goods and services, used to track inflation.
glossary.core inflation: Inflation excluding volatile food and energy prices, watched by central banks for the underlying trend.
glossary.PCE: Personal consumption expenditures price index: the US inflation measure the Federal Reserve targets.
glossary.GDP: Gross domestic product: the total value of goods and services an economy produces in a period.
glossary.recession: A significant, broad decline in economic activity; often approximated as two quarters of falling GDP.
glossary.stagflation: Slow growth combined with high inflation and often rising unemployment.
glossary.nonfarm payrolls: The monthly US count of jobs added outside farming, a closely watched sign of economic health.
glossary.VIX: The Cboe Volatility Index, which uses S&P 500 option prices to measure expected volatility; nicknamed the fear gauge.
glossary.short selling: Borrowing shares and selling them in the hope of buying them back cheaper later.
glossary.futures: Contracts to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a future date, used to hedge or speculate.
glossary.options: Contracts giving the right, but not the obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) an asset at a set price.
glossary.hedge fund: A lightly regulated investment fund for wealthy and institutional investors that uses strategies such as short selling and leverage.
glossary.private equity: Investment firms that buy companies, often with borrowed money, aiming to improve and sell them.
glossary.venture capital: Funding for young, high-risk companies in exchange for equity.
glossary.IPO: Initial public offering: when a private company first sells shares to the public and lists on a stock exchange.
glossary.guidance: A company's own forecast of future revenue or profit, which often moves its shares more than past results.
glossary.safe haven: An asset investors buy in times of stress, such as gold, US Treasuries or the Swiss franc.
glossary.Brent crude: The benchmark price for crude oil from the North Sea, used to price most of the world's oil.
glossary.WTI: West Texas Intermediate: the US benchmark crude oil price.
glossary.OPEC+: The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries plus allies such as Russia, which coordinate oil output.
glossary.stablecoin: A cryptocurrency designed to hold a steady value, usually one US dollar, backed by reserves.
glossary.dollar index: A measure of the US dollar against a basket of six major currencies.
glossary.carry trade: Borrowing in a low-interest currency, such as the yen, to invest in higher-yielding assets elsewhere.
glossary.credit rating: An agency's grade of how likely a borrower, such as a company or country, is to repay its debt.
glossary.liquidity: How easily an asset can be bought or sold without moving its price; also the amount of money available in the financial system.
glossary.Nifty 50: The NSE's benchmark index of 50 large Indian companies.
glossary.Sensex: The BSE's benchmark index of 30 large Indian companies, India's oldest stock index.
glossary.Bank Nifty: The NSE index of the most liquid Indian bank stocks; heavily traded in derivatives.
glossary.Dalal Street: The Mumbai street where the BSE stands; shorthand for the Indian stock market.
glossary.NSE: National Stock Exchange of India, the country's largest exchange by trading volume and home of the Nifty indices.
glossary.BSE: India's oldest stock exchange, in Mumbai, home of the Sensex.
glossary.SEBI: Securities and Exchange Board of India: the regulator of India's securities markets.
glossary.RBI: Reserve Bank of India: India's central bank, which sets interest rates, manages the rupee and regulates banks.
glossary.repo rate: The rate at which the RBI lends to banks overnight; its main policy rate and a driver of loan rates.
glossary.reverse repo rate: The rate at which the RBI borrows from banks, absorbing surplus money from the system.
glossary.standing deposit facility: The RBI window where banks park surplus funds overnight; it sets the floor of the policy corridor.
glossary.CRR: Cash reserve ratio: the share of deposits banks must keep with the RBI as cash, earning nothing.
glossary.SLR: Statutory liquidity ratio: the share of deposits banks must hold in safe assets such as government bonds.
glossary.MPC: The RBI's six-member Monetary Policy Committee, which votes on the repo rate.
glossary.FII: Foreign institutional investor; now officially foreign portfolio investor (FPI). Their daily buying or selling moves Indian markets.
glossary.DII: Domestic institutional investor, such as Indian mutual funds, insurers and pension funds.
glossary.F&O: Futures and options: the derivatives segment of Indian exchanges, where most trading by value happens.
glossary.expiry day: The day F&O contracts settle. Index expiries often bring sharp intraday swings.
glossary.circuit limit: The maximum a stock may rise or fall in a day, set by the exchange as a price band. A stock that hits it is said to be locked in the upper or lower circuit.
glossary.market-wide circuit breaker: A trading halt across the whole market when the Nifty or Sensex moves 10%, 15% or 20% in a day.
glossary.bhavcopy: The daily file an Indian exchange publishes with every security's open, high, low, close and volume.
glossary.T+1 settlement: Trades settle one working day after the trade date; India moved all stocks to T+1 in 2023.
glossary.T+0 settlement: Same-day settlement, offered as an optional cycle for a limited set of stocks.
glossary.ASM: Additional Surveillance Measure: a list of stocks with unusual price or volume moves on which exchanges impose stricter margins and limits.
glossary.GSM: Graded Surveillance Measure: exchange curbs on stocks whose prices look out of line with their fundamentals.
glossary.GMP: Grey market premium: the unofficial premium at which IPO shares trade before listing. It is unregulated and often wrong.
glossary.anchor investor: A large institution allotted IPO shares a day before the issue opens; their shares are locked in for a period.
glossary.QIB: Qualified institutional buyer, such as a mutual fund or bank; IPOs reserve a portion for them.
glossary.NII: Non-institutional investor, also called HNI: an individual applying for more than Rs 2 lakh of IPO shares.
glossary.SME IPO: A listing on the small and medium enterprise platforms of the NSE (Emerge) or BSE, with lighter rules and higher risk.
glossary.OFS: Offer for sale: existing shareholders, often promoters or the government, sell shares through the exchange or in an IPO.
glossary.QIP: Qualified institutional placement: a listed company raises money by selling new shares to institutions.
glossary.rights issue: An offer to existing shareholders to buy new shares, usually at a discount.
glossary.bonus issue: Free extra shares given to shareholders in proportion to their holdings.
glossary.stock split: Dividing each share into several, lowering the price per share without changing the company's value.
glossary.demat account: The electronic account in which Indian investors hold shares, kept with depositories NSDL or CDSL.
glossary.ASBA: Application supported by blocked amount: IPO money stays in the applicant's bank account, blocked, until shares are allotted.
glossary.SIP: Systematic investment plan: investing a fixed amount in a mutual fund every month.
glossary.AMFI: Association of Mutual Funds in India, the industry body that publishes monthly fund flows and SIP data.
glossary.NAV: Net asset value: the per-unit price of a mutual fund, calculated daily.
glossary.promoter: The founder or controlling shareholder group of an Indian listed company.
glossary.pledged shares: Shares a promoter has pledged as collateral for a loan; high pledging is a warning sign.
glossary.block deal: A single large trade done in a special exchange window, often between institutions.
glossary.India VIX: The NSE's volatility index, derived from Nifty option prices.
glossary.GIFT Nifty: Nifty futures traded at GIFT City in Gujarat, an early signal of where Indian markets will open; formerly SGX Nifty.
glossary.MCX: Multi Commodity Exchange of India, where gold, silver, crude oil and other commodity futures trade.
glossary.lakh and crore: Indian number units: one lakh is 100,000 and one crore is 10 million.
glossary.Muhurat trading: A short ceremonial trading session held on Diwali to mark the start of the Hindu new year.
glossary.STT: Securities transaction tax: a small tax charged on every purchase or sale of shares and derivatives in India.
glossary.capital gains tax: Tax on profit from selling investments. India taxes short-term (STCG) and long-term (LTCG) gains at different rates.
glossary.record date: The date on which a shareholder must be on the company's books to receive a dividend, bonus or split.
glossary.PSU: Public sector undertaking: a company majority-owned by the Indian government, such as SBI, ONGC or Coal India.
glossary.NBFC: Non-banking financial company: a lender that is not a bank, such as Bajaj Finance.
glossary.NPA: Non-performing asset: a loan on which interest or principal has been overdue for 90 days or more.
glossary.G-sec: Government security: a bond issued by the Indian central or state governments.
glossary.forex reserves: Foreign currency, gold and other reserve assets held by the RBI, used to steady the rupee.
glossary.FPI outflow: Net selling of Indian shares or bonds by foreign portfolio investors; large outflows weigh on the rupee and indices.
glossary.IPO subscription: How many times over an IPO's shares were applied for, reported separately for QIB, NII and retail portions.
glossary.Nifty Next 50: The NSE index of the 50 companies ranked just below the Nifty 50.
glossary.UPI: Unified Payments Interface: India's real-time payment system linking bank accounts through apps such as PhonePe, Google Pay and Paytm.
glossary.GST: Goods and services tax: India's nationwide indirect tax, with rates set by the GST Council.
